issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking declaratory and possessory relief concerning endowed property does not require compliance with the special procedure for suits concerning public charitable or religious trusts when it seeks none of the reliefs specified for such suits.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sued in a representative capacity concerning land they alleged had been endowed for a religious institution.
They sought declarations about the character of the land, the defendants’ interest in it, and the plaintiffs’ rights, as well as possession.
The plaint stated that a scheme might be sought later, but did not seek a scheme or another specified form of trust-administration relief.
issues.conclusion: The special procedure did not apply, and non-compliance with it did not make the suit unmaintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, § 92 applies to a suit presupposing a public charitable or religious trust and alleging breach of trust or the need for court directions, when the suit seeks at least one of the reliefs specified in that section. The declarations and possession sought here did not fall within those specified reliefs. The Court relied on Mahant Pragdasji Guru Bhagwandasji v. Patel Ishwarlalbhai Narsibhai, [1952] S.C.R. 513.

rule.if: civil_suit_concerning_endowed_property and (declaratory_relief_sought or possession_relief_sought) and no_specified_trust_relief_sought

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_endowed_property: The plaintiffs brought a civil suit concerning property alleged to be held for a public religious or charitable purpose.
predicates.declaratory_relief_sought: The plaintiffs sought a declaration concerning the character of the property or their rights in relation to it.
predicates.possession_relief_sought: The plaintiffs sought possession of the disputed property.
predicates.no_specified_trust_relief_sought: The plaintiffs did not seek any of the specified forms of relief concerning the appointment or removal of trustees, trust administration, or a trust scheme.

issues.definition: When a civil suit concerning endowed property seeks declarations or possession but no specified trust-administration relief, the special trust-suit procedure is not required.

issues.legal_issue: A grant made for the purpose of establishing and supporting a religious institution is an institutional religious endowment rather than a personal grant merely because it bears a label commonly associated with a personal grant.
material_facts: The grant was made contemporaneously with the establishment of a religious institution and appointment of its head priest.
The grant referred to the propagation of religious practice and was described as being for piety.
The lower courts interpreted the grant as serving the institution, relying on the text, other evidence, and their familiarity with the language and the local institutional and historical context.
The Supreme Court found no reason to reject that interpretation and considered the grant not to be personal to the priest and his family.
issues.conclusion: The grant was for the religious institution and its purposes, not a personal grant to the priest and his family; the term used in the grant did not change its essential character.
issues.legal_principle: The character of a grant is determined from its terms and the evidence in context; the label used for it does not alone determine whether it is personal or institutional. The Court declined to disturb the lower courts’ interpretation, noting their greater familiarity with the language, local institutions, and historical background. It distinguished Jibon Chandra Sarma Doloi v. Anand Ram Kalita, [1961] 3 S.C.R. 947, which concerned the effect of statutory revenue provisions on lands described as Brahmottar and did not decide the issue presented here.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_grant_interpretation and grant_tied_to_religious_institution and grant_states_institutional_religious_purpose and lower_courts_interpret_grant_as_institutional and local_context_supports_interpretation

predicates.appeal_challenges_grant_interpretation: A party in an appeal challenges the lower courts’ interpretation of a grant.
predicates.grant_tied_to_religious_institution: The grant was made in connection with the establishment or operation of a religious institution.
predicates.grant_states_institutional_religious_pur: The grant’s terms identify a religious purpose associated with the institution.
predicates.lower_courts_interpret_grant_as_institut: The lower courts interpreted the grant as serving the institution rather than benefiting its named recipient personally.
predicates.local_context_supports_interpretation: The lower courts’ interpretation is supported by evidence and their familiarity with the relevant language, institutions, or historical context.

issues.definition: When an appealed grant is tied to a religious institution, states an institutional religious purpose, and the lower courts’ institutional interpretation is supported by the local context, the grant is treated as an institutional religious endowment.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court need not consider a contention based on the legal effect of a land-tenure classification when that contention was not raised before the courts below.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the land’s tenure classification meant that the grant could be held only in a personal capacity.
The Supreme Court noted that this contention had not been raised before the High Court or any court below.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to allow the contention to be raised or to discuss its merits.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied no separately stated statutory provision or cited precedent to this point; it declined to entertain the contention because it had not been raised in the courts below.

predicates.appeal_in_civil_case: A party raises a contention in an appeal in a civil case.
predicates.tenure_based_argument_not_raised_below: The contention based on the legal effect of a land-tenure classification was not raised before the courts below.

issues.definition: When a tenure-based contention is first raised in a civil appeal after not being raised below, the contention is not considered.
